title: Norbert (6 June)
hook: a courtier knocked from his horse by lightning who founded the Premonstratensians

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kevin of Glendalough, and the bird in his open hand. Your line was the blackbird.

Lightning, on a country road. Below it, a rider in fine clothes, on his way somewhere that matters to him. A bolt strikes the ground in front of the horse, the horse rears, and the rider is thrown into the mud. He lies there, stunned, rain on his face, and, the story goes, he hears a voice. Yesterday's saint never moved. Today's saint gets moved, hard. Norbert.
screen: `A RIDER IN FINE CLOTHES.` → `LIGHTNING ON THE ROAD.` → `THROWN INTO THE MUD.`

segments.voice: Norbert was a nobleman and a cleric at court in the German lands, with a comfortable life and good connections. Tradition remembers him as worldly, holding church positions without much interest in what they were for. Then came the storm. Lying on the ground, in the story, he asked what Paul had asked: "Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?" The answer was a line from a psalm. In the Douay-Rheims: "Turn away from evil and do good." No vision of angels, no long speech. A line he'd have known by heart, suddenly aimed at him. The scene has an echo. Paintings show Paul thrown from a horse on the road to Damascus. But read Acts, and there's no horse. The Douay-Rheims says only: "And falling on the ground, he heard a voice." The horse comes from the painters. Norbert's story has a real one. He didn't change overnight into someone else. He did penance, was ordained a priest, and started preaching, barefoot, tradition says, from town to town. Then, at a remote place in France called Prémontré, he gathered men to live as canons: priests who pray the hours together like monks but go out to serve parishes. From that place comes his order's long name, the Premonstratensians, also called, more simply, the Norbertines. Later, as an archbishop, he worked to reform the clergy, the very kind of comfortable churchman he had once been. In his story, conversion is not one bright moment, but a fall, a question, and a long life of answering it.
screen: `A COMFORTABLE COURTIER.` · `THE QUESTION: WHAT WILT THOU HAVE ME DO?` · `PAUL'S HORSE IS NOT IN ACTS.` · `A FALL, THEN A LONG ANSWER.` · then, large: `TURN AWAY FROM EVIL AND DO GOOD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person caught in something that's hurting them, a habit or a hardness; maybe it's you. Hold them without lecturing, and wish them a good turning, in their own time. If you pray, ask quietly, as Norbert did, Lord, what wilt thou have me to do, and leave room for an answer.
Norbert. A courtier thrown to the ground in a storm, who turned, preached, and founded the Norbertines at Prémontré.
Your line: knocked from his horse. For Norbert, the storm was only the beginning. Day nine hundred ninety-eight, done.

howItsDone: Saint Norbert is remembered on 6 June; the Norbertine (Premonstratensian) canons and their parishes and schools keep it as their founder's feast, often with Mass and the Liturgy of the Hours sung together.

chat.meaning: Acts says only that Paul fell to the ground; the horse comes from the painters. Norbert, thrown in a storm, really had one.

notes: Conversion scene (lightning, thrown from horse, the question and the psalm answer) follows the traditional Vita Norberti; confirm the psalm line is the one tradition gives.
Acts 9:6 'Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?' is in the Douay-Rheims (from the Vulgate) though absent from some Greek manuscripts; confirm exact Challoner wording.
Psalm 33:15 in Douay-Rheims numbering (34:14 Hebrew numbering).
'Barefoot, tradition says': confirm. 'Later he became an archbishop' (Magdeburg) and reforming clergy: confirm wording.
Canons regular description ('pray the hours together like monks but go out to serve parishes'): confirm as fair.
Practice framed as a turning wished for someone, not proselytizing; Keeper to confirm tone.
